title: Der Fuchs und die Katze
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 75. Text from Wikisource (twice proofread against the original scans). 1857 spelling preserved (daß, gescheidt, theuren, Hochmuthes, bescheidentlich).
about: A fable of barely a page (KHM 75), and one whose kernel is far older than the collection — the cat with a single trick meets the fox who boasts of a hundred. He looks her over, calls her a whisker-washer and a starveling, and offers to teach her his craft; then the hounds come, and she is in the treetop while he is in their teeth. Watch the forms of address: she gives him a deferential ihr throughout, and keeps it up even when he is in the hounds’ teeth, while he answers with du. Spelling follows the 1857 edition (gescheidt, theuren, Hochmuthes, bescheidentlich).

sentences.t: Es trug sich zu, daß die Katze in einem Walde dem Herrn Fuchs begegnete, und weil sie dachte „er ist gescheidt und wohl erfahren, und gilt viel in der Welt,“ so sprach sie ihm freundlich zu.
sentences.l: It bore itself to pass that the cat in a forest met Mr. Fox, and because she thought “he is clever and well experienced, and counts for much in the world,” so she spoke to him amiably.
sentences.i: It came to pass that the cat met Mr. Fox in a forest; and because she thought, “He is clever and full of experience, and stands in high regard in the world,” she addressed him kindly.

sentences.t: „Guten Tag, lieber Herr Fuchs, wie gehts? wie stehts? wie schlagt ihr euch durch in dieser theuren Zeit?“
sentences.l: “Good day, dear Mr. Fox, how goes it? how stands it? how do you beat yourself through in this dear time?”
sentences.i: “Good day, dear Mr. Fox — how goes it? how stands it? how are you making your way through these costly times?”
sentences.n: gehts and stehts are geht es and steht es run together. “sich durchschlagen” = to get by, scrape through. theuren is the 1857 spelling of teuren: a theure Zeit is a season of high prices and short food. She addresses him with the deferential ihr (“schlagt ihr euch”); his reply will use du.

sentences.t: Der Fuchs, alles Hochmuthes voll, betrachtete die Katze von Kopf bis zu Füßen und wußte lange nicht ob er eine Antwort geben sollte.
sentences.l: The fox, full of all haughtiness, looked at the cat from head to feet and knew for a long time not whether he should give an answer.
sentences.i: The fox, brimming with arrogance, looked the cat over from head to foot, and for a long while did not know whether he should give an answer at all.

sentences.t: Endlich sprach er „O du armseliger Bartputzer, du buntscheckiger Narr, du Hungerleider und Mäusejäger, was kommt dir in den Sinn? du unterstehst dich zu fragen wie mirs gehe?
sentences.l: At last spoke he “O you wretched beard-cleaner, you motley fool, you hunger-sufferer and mouse-hunter, what comes into your mind? you dare to ask how it goes with me?
sentences.i: At last he spoke: “Oh, you miserable whisker-washer, you piebald fool, you starveling and mouse-catcher — what has got into your head? You presume to ask how I am faring?
sentences.n: A string of coined insults: Bartputzer, a “beard-cleaner” (the cat forever washing her whiskers); buntscheckig, motley or piebald; Hungerleider, one who suffers hunger, a starveling. gehe is subjunctive because the question is reported — he throws her own words back at her.

sentences.t: was hast du gelernt? wie viel Künste verstehst du?“
sentences.l: what have you learned? how many arts do you understand?”
sentences.i: What have you learned? How many arts do you know?”
sentences.n: Kunst here is not art in our sense but a skill, a trick, a piece of craft — the word carries the whole fable, and the cat and the fox count theirs against each other to the end.

sentences.t: „Ich verstehe nur eine einzige“ antwortete bescheidentlich die Katze.
sentences.l: “I understand only a single one,” answered modestly the cat.
sentences.i: “I know only a single one,” the cat answered modestly.

sentences.t: „Was ist das für eine Kunst?“ fragte der Fuchs.
sentences.l: “What is that for an art?” asked the fox.
sentences.i: “And what sort of art is that?” asked the fox.

sentences.t: „Wenn die Hunde hinter mir her sind, so kann ich auf einen Baum springen und mich retten.“
sentences.l: “When the dogs are behind me in pursuit, so can I spring up a tree and save myself.”
sentences.i: “When the hounds are after me, I can spring up a tree and save myself.”

sentences.t: „Ist das alles?“ sagte der Fuchs, „ich bin Herr über hundert Künste und habe überdies noch einen Sack voll Liste.
sentences.l: “Is that all?” said the fox, “I am master over a hundred arts and have besides that a sack full of cunning.
sentences.i: “Is that all?” said the fox. “I am master of a hundred arts, and I have a whole sackful of guile besides.
sentences.n: Liste here belongs to die List (cunning, a ruse), not the modern Liste “list”: “ein Sack voll Liste” is a sack full of guile. The sack turns literal a few lines on, when the cat tells him to open it.

sentences.t: Du jammerst mich, komm mit mir, ich will dich lehren wie man den Hunden entgeht.“
sentences.l: You grieve me, come with me, I will teach you how one gets away from the dogs.”
sentences.i: You move me to pity — come with me, and I will teach you how to escape the hounds.”
sentences.n: “du jammerst mich” inverts the English arrangement: the one pitied is the subject and the one who pities is the object — “you make me sorry for you.” entgehen (to escape, get away from) takes the dative: den Hunden.

sentences.t: Indem kam ein Jäger mit vier Hunden daher.
sentences.l: In that moment came a hunter with four dogs along.
sentences.i: Just then a hunter came along with four hounds.
sentences.n: indem here is temporal — just then, in that very moment — not the modern conjunction “by doing.”

sentences.t: Die Katze sprang behend auf einen Baum und setzte sich in den Gipfel, wo Äste und Laubwerk sie völlig verbargen.
sentences.l: The cat sprang nimbly up a tree and set herself in the summit, where branches and foliage concealed her completely.
sentences.i: The cat sprang nimbly up a tree and settled in the crown, where boughs and leafage hid her entirely.

sentences.t: „Bindet den Sack auf, Herr Fuchs, bindet den Sack auf,“ rief ihm die Katze zu, aber die Hunde hatten ihn schon gepackt und hielten ihn fest.
sentences.l: “Untie the sack, Mr. Fox, untie the sack,” called the cat to him, but the dogs had already seized him and held him fast.
sentences.i: “Open your sack, Mr. Fox, open your sack!” the cat called down to him — but the hounds had already seized him and were holding him fast.
sentences.n: aufbinden = to untie, to undo the string of; the imperative bindet is the ihr-form she has used for him all along. She is asking him to open his sack of a hundred arts as though it were a real sack.

sentences.t: „Ei, Herr Fuchs,“ rief die Katze, „ihr bleibt mit euern hundert Künsten stecken.
sentences.l: “Ei, Mr. Fox,” cried the cat, “you remain stuck with your hundred arts.
sentences.i: “Well, Mr. Fox,” cried the cat, “there you stick, with your hundred arts and all.
sentences.n: “stecken bleiben” = to be stuck, to get no further — and here also literally caught fast. euern is an older spelling of euren.

sentences.t: Hättet ihr heraufkriechen können wie ich, so wärs nicht um euer Leben geschehen.“
sentences.l: Had you been able to creep up here as I, so it would not be over with your life.”
sentences.i: Had you been able to climb up here as I did, it would not now be all over with your life.”
sentences.n: “es ist um etwas geschehen” = it is all up with something, it is lost. The condition carries no wenn — “Hättet ihr…” = “Had you…,” exactly as English can do it. wärs = wäre es.
